# Reviewing metalquicha

A Fortran 2003+ quantum chemistry code: fragment-based methods (MBE, GMBE, FMO)
over three engines — tblite for xTB, libfint/libcint for CPU Gaussian integrals,
cuEST for GPU. MPI across fragments, OpenMP within one.

`AGENTS.md` describes the project. This file is narrower: what tends to go wrong
here, so a review spends its attention where the bugs actually are.

## The failure that matters most

**A wrong number that still converges.** Almost nothing in this codebase fails
loudly. A misplaced factor, a dropped term or a partition applied at the wrong
level produces a calculation that finishes, prints a plausible energy, and is
wrong — one such bug was 11 Hartree off and looked entirely normal in the log.

So the question for any change touching numerics is not "does this run" but
"what would it look like if this were wrong, and would anything notice". Prefer
review comments that name a concrete input where the change gives a different
answer over comments about style.

**Energies must not move.** A refactor, an optimisation or a threading change
must leave energies identical to roundoff — 1e-12 to 1e-10 depending on the
quantity. A PR claiming to be performance-only that shifts a validated energy in
the sixth decimal has changed the method, whatever the description says.

## Things that have actually broken here

**OpenMP `private` on a derived type.** A private copy is not guaranteed to pick
up default initialisation. A `type(error_t)` declared `private` came through
with a nonzero error code, so every block reported failure and the result was
silently zero. Use `firstprivate` to copy in a clean value. Clearing it inside
the region is worse — the clear deallocates components that were never
allocated.

**Leaving an OpenMP region early.** A thread cannot `return` out of one, and the
barrier at the end has to be reached by all of them. Failures inside a parallel
region must set a flag and be handled after.

**MPI error paths that skip a collective.** If one rank hits an error and
returns while the others wait at an `allreduce`, the job hangs. Errors detected
on one rank have to travel *through* the reduction, not around it.

**Two build systems that find sources differently.** CMake lists sources
explicitly in each `CMakeLists.txt`; fpm walks `src/` by convention. A file
generated into the build tree is invisible to fpm, and a file added to `src/`
without being listed is invisible to CMake. Adding either kind breaks one build
and not the other, and CI may only cover one.

**Tests registered outside their backend guard.** `test/CMakeLists.txt` wraps
libcint-dependent tests in `if(MQC_ENABLE_CZT)`. A test using
`mqc_czt_*` modules registered outside it breaks every reduced build with
`Cannot open module file`. Check which modules a new test `use`s, not where its
`addtest` line happens to sit.

**Hand-added validation decks.** Everything under `validation/inputs/cpu/mqc/`
is generated by `tools/cpu_validation/gen_cpu_validation.py`, which deletes
decks it did not write. A deck added by hand needs an entry in `HAND_MAINTAINED`
*and* its manifest entry survives only through the read-back — both, or it is
silently dropped and the coverage looks present while no longer running.

**Scatter indices.** `frag%atoms` maps a fragment onto the system and is used as
an array index in several places. Anything appended to it that is not a real
system atom writes out of bounds. Ghost and cap atoms live in the coordinate and
element arrays and never in `atoms`.

## Fortran rules this project enforces

* every `use` has an `only` clause — `fortitude check` fails CI otherwise
* no `GOTO`, arithmetic `IF`, implicit `SAVE`, `COMMON`, `EQUIVALENCE`,
  fixed-form source or assumed-size arrays
* no `block` construct inside an OpenMP region — nvfortran rejects it
  (NVFORTRAN-S-1219); declare at routine scope and privatise
* don't name a variable `close` — fortitude parses it as the statement, reports
  a syntax error, and then discards every other finding in that file
* internal units are Bohr and Hartree; convert with `to_bohr` / `to_angstrom`

## Performance claims

Treat a timing in a PR description as unverified unless it says how many runs it
is a median of. Measured here: DFT energies repeat to under one per cent, while
gradients dominated by a serial loop varied by sixteen — a single-shot
comparison across that produced a phantom twenty per cent regression that did
not exist.

Two more things a performance change should have thought about:

* **Fragmented and unfragmented workloads pull in opposite directions.**
  Fragment paths pin themselves to one OpenMP thread and parallelise over MPI.
  A change that speeds up a single molecule can slow the fragment path down —
  switching to a threaded BLAS was five times faster on one molecule and
  thirty-one per cent slower on four ranks. A PR that only measured one of them
  has only measured half.
* **Thread at this project's level, not the library's.** Our own OpenMP respects
  `omp_set_num_threads`, so the same code threads on an unfragmented run and
  stays serial inside a pinned fragment worker. A threaded BLAS underneath does
  not.

## CMake

`CMAKE_STYLE.md` has the rules; these are the three worth stopping a PR over.

- **A `FetchContent_Declare` outside `cmake/modules/MqcFetch.cmake`.** Every
  dependency is declared in its own `cmake/modules/Find<pkg>.cmake` through
  `mqc_fetch`, with its pin and the reason for that pin beside it.
- **An `option()` anywhere but `cmake/MqcOptions.cmake`.** One declared at its
  point of use is declared too late for anything read earlier: that is how the
  ECP matrix test came to be gated on a variable that did not exist yet, and so
  never ran at all while the suite reported success.
- **Growth in the top-level `CMakeLists.txt`.** It is an outline -- four
  includes and the targets between them. Anything added there has a file it
  belongs in instead.

Also: a branch as a `GIT_TAG` (a moving pin reddens the matrix with a signal
indistinguishable from a real break), and a validation program added by hand
rather than through `mqc_add_validation_program`.

## Style

Comments explain *why*, not what. The codebase documents the decision, the
alternative that was rejected and the measurement behind it; a comment
restating the code adds nothing. The same goes for a PR description.

Prefer flagging a missing *reason* over a missing comment. "This is a magic
number" is a weaker review comment than "where does 0.35 come from, and what
happens at 0.5" — which in that case was the difference between working code and
counting core orbitals as bonds.
